questions.q: Which description best characterizes basal cell carcinoma on skin examination?
ch: A firm, scaly, hyperkeratotic and often tender ulcerated nodule on sun-exposed skin
A pearly, translucent papule with rolled borders and telangiectasias, sometimes centrally ulcerated
A chronic non-healing ulcer arising within an old burn scar on the lower leg
A well-demarcated scaly plaque representing full-thickness in-situ change
A rough, sandpaper-like erythematous macule that is felt more easily than it is seen

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the metastatic behavior of BCC and cutaneous SCC?
ch: Both BCC and SCC metastasize in roughly 2-5% of cases and are therefore managed identically
SCC essentially never metastasizes while BCC spreads to regional nodes in most patients
BCC metastasizes in about 2-5% of cases and SCC in fewer than 0.1% of cases
Neither tumor is capable of metastasis, so neither one requires any risk stratification
BCC metastasizes rarely (<0.1%) but is locally destructive, whereas SCC metastasizes in roughly 2-5% of cases

questions.q: Actinic keratosis is best described as which of the following?
ch: A rough, sandpaper-like erythematous macule on the precursor spectrum leading to SCC
A benign lesion with no relationship to skin cancer that requires no treatment at all
Squamous cell carcinoma in situ, which carries the specific name Bowen disease
A pearly papule showing arborizing vessels when examined with dermoscopy
A locally destructive tumor driven by PTCH1 mutation in the Hedgehog pathway

questions.q: A 68-year-old has a biopsy-proven basal cell carcinoma with ill-defined borders on the nasal ala. Which treatment does the module identify as preferred?
ch: Cryotherapy to the clinically apparent border
Vismodegib, a Hedgehog pathway inhibitor
Electrodesiccation and curettage of the visible lesion
Mohs micrographic surgery for complete margin control
Topical 5-fluorouracil applied as field therapy

questions.q: A skin biopsy shows basaloid nests with peripheral palisading and retraction clefting. What is the diagnosis?
ch: Marjolin ulcer arising in a chronic burn scar
Squamous cell carcinoma, based on keratin pearls
Actinic keratosis, the precursor spectrum lesion
Bowen disease, squamous cell carcinoma in situ
Basal cell carcinoma, most often the nodular subtype

questions.q: A patient starting topical 5-fluorouracil for actinic keratoses asks what to expect. Which counseling point does the module specify?
ch: It works by blocking the Hedgehog pathway and causes muscle spasms and dysgeusia
It is appropriate first-line therapy for a nodular basal cell carcinoma on the nose
Brisk erythema and erosion are an expected therapeutic reaction, and the treated area needs sun protection
The drug is safe in pregnancy and requires no additional precautions
Any redness means an allergic reaction and the cream should be stopped at once

questions.q: Which set of features identifies a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma as high-risk and drives workup or adjuvant therapy?
ch: A pearly translucent appearance with rolled borders and arborizing vessels on dermoscopy
Palmar pits, jaw keratocysts and multiple basal cell carcinomas of early onset
Size >2 cm, depth >2 mm, poor differentiation, perineural invasion, ear or lip location, immunosuppression, recurrence
Sandpaper-like texture across a broad field of erythematous macules on a bald scalp
Defective nucleotide excision repair with severe photosensitivity beginning in childhood

questions.q: A kidney transplant recipient on chronic immunosuppression has a rapidly enlarging, ulcerating squamous cell carcinoma on the ear with new numbness in the area. Which approach matches the module?
ch: Treat with cryotherapy because the ear is a cosmetically sensitive site that should be spared surgery
Treat this as high-risk SCC — new numbness suggests perineural invasion — and consider reducing immunosuppression with aggressive surveillance
Reassure him that SCC in transplant recipients behaves like SCC in anyone else and simply observe the lesion
Begin topical imiquimod, since an immune modulator is the logical choice for invasive disease in this setting
Start anti-PD-1 immunotherapy immediately as first-line therapy without regard to his allograft

questions.q: A 22-year-old with multiple basal cell carcinomas, jaw keratocysts and palmar pits is offered treatment options. Why does the module caution against radiation therapy for him?
ch: Radiation predictably causes muscle spasms, dysgeusia and alopecia in patients with this syndrome
Radiation would provoke immune-related adverse events and put a transplanted allograft at risk of rejection
Radiation provides no histologic margin confirmation, so it is never an acceptable option for any basal cell carcinoma
Radiation should be avoided in young patients and in genetic syndromes such as basal cell nevus syndrome because of secondary tumor risk
Radiation is a recognized teratogen and demands the same strict contraception required with Hedgehog inhibitors

questions.q: You are presenting a patient with a 1 cm pearly papule with a rolled border and telangiectasias on the nose. What does the module say to state next?
ch: That you are most concerned about a nodular BCC and biopsy is definitive, then recommend Mohs for this facial site
That empiric topical 5-fluorouracil should be started and the lesion reassessed in three months
That dermoscopy showing arborizing vessels has established the diagnosis and no biopsy is needed
That imaging and laboratory studies should be ordered to stage the lesion before any treatment
That a sentinel lymph node biopsy should be arranged given the metastatic risk of this lesion

questions.q: What is the diagnostic hallmark of ordinary urticaria?
ch: Dusky targetoid macules with mucosal erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign
Painful, burning lesions that persist for several days and leave bruising behind
Migratory, intensely pruritic wheals in which each individual lesion resolves within 24 hours
Deep, non-pruritic swelling of the lips and tongue occurring without any wheals
Fixed, sharply demarcated erythematous plaques confined to the site of contact

questions.q: By the definition used in this module, urticaria is called chronic when wheals recur most days for at least how long?
ch: 24 hours
1 week
4 weeks
6 weeks
6 months

questions.q: Which mechanism produces the wheals of urticaria?
ch: Mast-cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, causing superficial dermal edema
Bradykinin accumulation producing deep swelling without itch or wheals
Cytotoxic T cells releasing granulysin and causing keratinocyte apoptosis
Direct chemical injury to keratinocytes from an external irritant agent
Leukocytoclastic vasculitis of small dermal vessels with immune complex deposition

questions.q: A patient with chronic spontaneous urticaria asks which medication should form the backbone of her therapy. What does the module recommend first-line?
ch: Montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist, as initial monotherapy
A scheduled second-generation H1 antihistamine such as cetirizine, loratadine or fexofenadine
First-generation diphenhydramine taken only on the days when itching flares
A short prednisone burst continued indefinitely as maintenance therapy
Famotidine used as single-agent H2 receptor blockade

questions.q: A woman with chronic spontaneous urticaria remains symptomatic on a standard dose of cetirizine. According to the guideline ladder in the module, what is the next step?
ch: Add a systemic corticosteroid for long-term maintenance control
Switch to hydroxyzine because sedating agents control wheals better
Up-dose the second-generation antihistamine to as much as 4x the standard dose
Start omalizumab immediately before adjusting the antihistamine dose
Order a broad allergy panel and defer any change in her therapy

questions.q: Which set of findings should prompt a skin biopsy for urticarial vasculitis rather than reassurance about ordinary hives?
ch: Lesions lasting more than 24 hours that are painful or burning and resolve with purpura
Deep swelling of the lips without wheals in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor
Blanching wheals with pale centers that move from site to site each day
Small punctate wheals appearing with exercise, heat, or emotional sweating
A linear wheal that appears within minutes of stroking the skin

questions.q: A patient reports linear welts wherever her skin is scratched or where a bag strap presses. Which office test does the module list to confirm this form?
ch: Skin-prick testing with a standard broad aeroallergen panel
Patch testing applied to the back and read at 48 and 96 hours
Measuring serum complement levels and inflammatory markers
Applying an ice cube to the forearm and observing for a wheal
Stroking the skin to elicit a linear wheal, confirming dermographism

questions.q: A man develops hives after a new antibiotic and now has wheezing, vomiting and light-headedness. What is the immediate priority?
ch: Give IV diphenhydramine and observe the response
Start a scheduled second-generation H1 antihistamine
Administer a prednisone burst as the primary intervention
Arrange outpatient omalizumab as soon as possible
Give IM epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh

questions.q: A patient on lisinopril has isolated lip and tongue swelling with no wheals and no itch, and has not improved with antihistamines. What does the module say explains this?
ch: Urticarial vasculitis, which requires a skin biopsy and complement levels
Bradykinin-mediated angioedema, which does not respond to antihistamines or epinephrine the way histaminergic disease does
Histamine acting at H1 receptors, so the antihistamine should simply be up-dosed to four times the standard dose
Chronic spontaneous urticaria of an autoimmune type that will respond to add-on omalizumab
Cholinergic urticaria triggered by heat, exercise, and emotional sweating

questions.q: A patient with refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria is starting omalizumab. Which monitoring point does the module emphasize?
ch: Taper the drug over two to three weeks to prevent rebound urticaria
Check a broad food allergy panel before each subcutaneous dose
Expect a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events and screen for mood change
Observe the patient after the subcutaneous injection because of anaphylaxis risk
Monitor renal function and blood pressure at every visit while on therapy

questions.q: How are SJS, SJS/TEN overlap, and TEN distinguished from one another?
ch: By the depth of the split, subcorneal in SJS and full thickness in TEN
By the SCORTEN score, with TEN defined as a score greater than four
By body surface area of epidermal detachment: SJS <10%, overlap 10-30%, TEN >30%
By the number of mucosal surfaces involved, with TEN requiring three or more sites
By whether the trigger is a drug, meaning TEN, or an infection, meaning SJS

questions.q: Which immunologic mechanism underlies SJS/TEN?
ch: Autoantibodies against desmosomal proteins with positive direct immunofluorescence
Type IV T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity with granulysin driving keratinocyte apoptosis
Immune complex deposition causing leukocytoclastic vasculitis of dermal vessels
Direct chemical injury to keratinocytes from an exogenous irritant agent
Type I IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation with histamine release

questions.q: Which drug does the module name as the single most common cause of SJS/TEN worldwide?
ch: Lamotrigine, one of the anticonvulsant culprits
An oxicam NSAID such as piroxicam
Carbamazepine, especially in HLA-B*15:02 carriers
Allopurinol, often started for asymptomatic hyperuricemia
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, a sulfonamide antibiotic

questions.q: A patient develops painful dusky macules and oral erosions. Which exposure window does the module use to identify the culprit drug?
ch: Only after the drug has already been stopped
Within minutes to two hours of the first dose
Within 24 to 48 hours of starting the drug
Only after continuous use for more than one year
4 to 28 days after the drug was started

questions.q: A child has diffuse superficial peeling with a positive Nikolsky sign but no mucosal involvement, and biopsy shows a subcorneal split. What does the module identify?
ch: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, which splits subcorneally and spares mucosa
Toxic epidermal necrolysis with more than 30% detachment
SJS/TEN overlap with 10-30% detachment
Erythema multiforme major from an infectious trigger
An autoimmune blistering disease with positive direct immunofluorescence

questions.q: A patient with TEN triggered by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has wound care orders written. Which order should you question?
ch: Silver sulfadiazine applied to the denuded areas
Frequent ophthalmic lubrication with an urgent ophthalmology consult
Pre-medication with opioid analgesia before dressing changes
Nanocrystalline silver non-adherent dressings
Petrolatum-based non-stick dressings

questions.q: On rounds you are asked why you favor early cyclosporine over late systemic corticosteroids in TEN. Which answer matches the module?
ch: Cyclosporine has no laboratory monitoring requirements at all, which makes it the safer choice in any patient
IVIG has demonstrated clear superiority over both agents in trials and should be substituted for either one
Corticosteroids are effective only in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and have no role at all in necrolysis
Cyclosporine is increasingly favored as first-line adjunctive therapy, while steroids may raise infection and mortality risk if given late or prolonged
Systemic steroids are contraindicated in this setting because they are teratogenic, whereas cyclosporine carries no such risk

questions.q: Which combination of findings would worsen a TEN patient’s SCORTEN and prompt escalation of care?
ch: A urine output at the target set for fluid resuscitation
Age under 40 with a normal bicarbonate and a heart rate of 80
A negative Nikolsky sign with fewer than two mucosal sites involved
Negative direct immunofluorescence on the diagnostic skin biopsy
Rising BUN, a heart rate above 120, and a falling bicarbonate

questions.q: How does fluid management in TEN differ from that of a thermal burn of similar body surface area?
ch: Requirements are identical, so standard burn formulas can be applied unchanged
TEN requires substantially more fluid because losses through denuded skin are greater
TEN requires less fluid than a thermal burn, and over-resuscitation risks pulmonary edema
Fluids should be withheld entirely and losses replaced by the enteral route
Fluid volume is dictated by the SCORTEN score rather than by clinical response

questions.q: A patient recovering from carbamazepine-induced SJS is being prepared for discharge. Which two measures does the module emphasize?
ch: Sentinel lymph node sampling of the involved regions, followed by lifelong scheduled antihistamine therapy
Lifelong avoidance of the culprit and cross-reactive drugs with a medical alert bracelet, plus HLA-B*15:02 screening to prevent future cases
Cautiously restart the drug at a lower dose under close observation, with weekly laboratory monitoring thereafter
Lifelong avoidance of all live vaccines, with a repeat diagnostic skin biopsy arranged in three months
Indefinite systemic corticosteroids at a maintenance dose, together with strict avoidance of all NSAIDs

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes irritant contact dermatitis?
ch: It is the most common form, a non-immune direct cytotoxic injury that anyone exposed to enough irritant develops
It is an IgE-mediated type I reaction best confirmed with skin-prick testing and serum IgE
It is a type IV delayed cell-mediated hypersensitivity that requires prior sensitization to the agent
It accounts for roughly 20% of cases and develops only in individuals who have been sensitized
It is the form confirmed by patch testing applied to the back and read at 48 and 72-96 hours

questions.q: Which bedside discriminator does the module give for separating allergic from irritant contact dermatitis?
ch: Allergic disease burns immediately on contact while irritant disease itches only after several days have passed
Irritant disease burns and is sharply demarcated; allergic disease itches and peaks at 24-72 hours, spreading beyond the contact site
Only allergic disease produces vesicles, because irritant disease never blisters, weeps, or becomes eroded
Irritant disease requires prior sensitization to the agent whereas allergic disease can occur on first exposure
Allergic disease is confirmed by a KOH preparation taken from the advancing edge of the lesion

questions.q: A hiker develops intensely itchy linear streaks of vesicles on his forearms two days after clearing brush. What does this pattern indicate?
ch: Nickel allergy from a metal watch strap
Irritant dermatitis from repetitive wet work
Poison ivy or oak urushiol contact, a type IV hypersensitivity
Neomycin sensitization at a healing wound edge
Para-phenylenediamine reaction from hair dye

questions.q: Which statement about patch testing matches the module?
ch: Reactions are graded on the SCORTEN scale from one through seven
Allergens are applied to the back, read at 48 h and again at 72-96 h, and positives must be clinically relevant
A single reading taken at 24 hours after application is sufficient to capture all reactions
It is the confirmatory gold standard for diagnosing irritant contact dermatitis
A positive reaction is clinically relevant by definition and requires no correlation with exposure

questions.q: A patient has allergic contact dermatitis of the eyelids from a new cosmetic. Which choice matches the module’s site-based approach?
ch: High-potency clobetasol applied twice daily to the eyelids until the rash clears
A five-day course of oral prednisone stopped abruptly without any taper
Oral diphenhydramine used as the sole treatment for the eruption
Dupilumab started immediately as the initial steroid-sparing measure
A topical calcineurin inhibitor such as tacrolimus, with low-potency steroid if a steroid is used

questions.q: A parent asks whether her child’s poison ivy blisters will spread the rash to siblings. What is the correct teaching?
ch: Spread indicates a secondary bacterial infection requiring oral antibiotics
The blister fluid is contagious, so the child should be isolated until the vesicles dry
Vesicle fluid does not spread the rash; new lesions come from residual urushiol or delayed absorption
New lesions prove an ongoing type I IgE-mediated allergy and require prick testing
The rash spreads only if the child scratches, so antihistamines alone will stop it

questions.q: A patient’s minor laceration keeps worsening with increasing itch and vesicles at the wound edges while she applies triple antibiotic ointment. What should you suspect?
ch: Cellulitis requiring oral antibiotic therapy
Irritant dermatitis from the wound dressing adhesive
Tinea, which a KOH preparation would confirm
Allergic contact dermatitis to neomycin or bacitracin, frequent sensitizers
A phototoxic reaction at a sun-exposed site

questions.q: A patient with extensive poison ivy involving the face is given oral prednisone. What does the module say about the course?
ch: Pair it with a KOH prep before every dose adjustment
Give a single dose and rely on topical steroids thereafter
Continue it indefinitely to prevent recurrence after future exposure
Taper over 2-3 weeks, because short courses cause rebound
Avoid systemic corticosteroids entirely in contact dermatitis

questions.q: A patient being treated for presumed contact dermatitis now has oral erosions, targetoid lesions and skin sloughing. What does the module direct you to consider?
ch: SJS/TEN, erythema multiforme or angioedema rather than simple contact dermatitis
A stronger topical corticosteroid applied to the affected areas
Extended patch testing to identify additional relevant allergens
A KOH preparation to exclude a dermatophyte infection
A trial of a topical calcineurin inhibitor for the mucosal lesions

questions.q: A machinist with chronic hand dermatitis gets only partial relief from topical steroids. Which intervention does the module identify as the definitive one?
ch: Increasing the topical corticosteroid potency indefinitely and continuing it long-term
Adding a sedating oral antihistamine at bedtime for symptomatic relief
Starting cyclosporine as the first-line treatment for his hand disease
Confirming the diagnosis with serum IgE and skin-prick testing
Identifying and avoiding the allergen or irritant, with barrier repair using emollients and protective gloves

questions.q: Which set of factors does the module identify as the pathophysiology of acne vulgaris?
ch: Follicular hyperkeratinization, androgen-driven sebum overproduction, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, and inflammation
A type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a sebaceous antigen with memory T-cell activation
Mast-cell histamine release producing follicular edema, wheals, and intense pruritus
Cumulative ultraviolet damage to keratinocytes driving p53 pyrimidine-dimer mutation
Autoantibodies directed at the sebaceous gland with positive direct immunofluorescence

questions.q: What accounts for the dark color of an open comedone (blackhead)?
ch: Trapped dirt that responds to vigorous scrubbing
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation from prior nodules
Oxidized keratin and melanin within the open follicular plug
Hemosiderin deposition from ruptured follicular vessels
Minocycline-induced pigment deposition in the dermis

questions.q: A teenager has purely comedonal acne with blackheads and whiteheads and no inflammatory lesions. What is first-line therapy?
ch: Topical clindamycin used as single-agent monotherapy
A topical retinoid such as tretinoin or adapalene, applied at night
Spironolactone combined with an oral contraceptive pill
Oral doxycycline given for a three-to-four month course
Oral isotretinoin under iPLEDGE with monthly pregnancy testing

questions.q: Why does the module insist that every topical or oral antibiotic for acne be paired with benzoyl peroxide?
ch: Benzoyl peroxide replaces the need to limit oral antibiotic courses in time
Benzoyl peroxide neutralizes the photosensitivity caused by the tetracyclines
Benzoyl peroxide kills C. acnes without promoting resistance, so pairing prevents antibiotic resistance
Benzoyl peroxide is required to keep the antibiotic from bleaching fabrics and hair
Benzoyl peroxide is needed to protect against pseudotumor cerebri

questions.q: A 7-year-old is brought in with inflammatory acne and the family asks about doxycycline. Which concern applies?
ch: Tetracyclines must be paired with a combined oral contraceptive
Tetracyclines cause potassium retention requiring serial monitoring
Tetracyclines are comedolytic and normalize follicular keratinization
Tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 8 because of tooth staining
Tetracyclines require iPLEDGE enrollment and monthly pregnancy tests

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman has sudden severe acne along the jawline with hirsutism and irregular menses. What does the module advise?
ch: Reassure her that adult-onset acne requires no additional laboratory evaluation
Begin oral isotretinoin immediately without any baseline laboratory testing
Order patch testing to identify a cosmetic allergen as the underlying cause
Perform a KOH preparation of a pustule to exclude fungal folliculitis
Screen for hyperandrogenism and PCOS with total and free testosterone and DHEA-S, considering LH/FSH

questions.q: A patient on isotretinoin develops a severe headache with blurred vision. Which combination does the module warn causes this, and what should be done?
ch: Isotretinoin plus spironolactone; check a potassium level and continue
Isotretinoin plus a tetracycline causes pseudotumor cerebri; stop and evaluate immediately
Isotretinoin plus a topical retinoid; reduce the topical to alternate nights
Isotretinoin plus a combined oral contraceptive; discontinue the contraceptive
Isotretinoin plus benzoyl peroxide; stop the benzoyl peroxide only

questions.q: On rounds you are asked why isotretinoin can produce durable remission when other agents cannot. What is the module’s reasoning?
ch: It permanently eradicates C. acnes from the follicle through a purely bactericidal mechanism
It blocks androgen receptors in the sebaceous gland in the same way that spironolactone does
It acts purely as a comedolytic agent and requires no other mechanism to be effective
Its long half-life maintains therapeutic drug levels in the skin for years after the course ends
It uniquely hits all four pathogenic factors — shrinking sebaceous glands, normalizing keratinization, reducing C. acnes, and anti-inflammatory action

questions.q: A teenager develops abrupt ulcerating hemorrhagic nodules with fever, arthralgia and leukocytosis. What does the module call this and how is it handled?
ch: Gram-negative folliculitis; stop all antibiotics and observe
Nodulocystic acne; begin isotretinoin at the usual starting dose
Perioral dermatitis; switch to a low-potency topical steroid
Acne fulminans, a dermatologic emergency requiring systemic steroids
Rosacea flare; start topical metronidazole and avoid triggers

questions.q: A patient starting a topical retinoid returns after three weeks frustrated that her skin is drier and looks worse. Which counseling matches the module?
ch: Topical results take 8-12 weeks and initial dryness and purging are expected, so continue and use sunscreen
She should scrub her face more vigorously to clear the blackheads more quickly
She should switch to applying the retinoid in the morning instead, to reduce dryness
The worsening indicates an allergic reaction and she needs patch testing to confirm it
The retinoid has failed at three weeks and should be replaced with an oral antibiotic
